title: Christ Casts Out the Tyrant
english: … peoples of the Savior, those sanctified (through the Spirit, that is) and cleansed through faith, he leapt upon terribly and bitterly. He made war on the Church of God, shaking at her the most unholy phalanx of the spirits under his hand. Perhaps he even thought he could overturn her with very little effort, the truly venerable and holy city of God, the spiritual Jerusalem. But he was caught, for none of his plans was possible. He could not besiege and take the holy city, or overpower a right hand so very strong. For who will stand against God, who can do all things?

So he perished together with his own shield-bearers, and was driven away from the flock of the godly, though he sprang on it like a savage beast; and he has been cast out of his tyranny over us. The Savior taught us this when he said: “Now is the judgment of this age; now the ruler of this age will be cast out. And I, if I am lifted up on the earth, will draw all to myself” (John 12:31–32). For the passion of Christ became the overthrow of death, the pulling down of the devil, and the destruction of sin: he was lifted up on the cross, and he brought down the devil’s boast and threw it to the ground.

In due time, then, after those events, the God of all now brings in the account of the Only-Begotten’s birth according to the flesh, and reveals the mystery beforehand through the voice of prophets, so that when the events came to fulfillment, it might be believed by all without dispute. What, then, does he say? “Behold, the Master, the Lord of Hosts, will throw the glorious into confusion with strength” (Isaiah 10:33).

The mystery of Christ refashions those on earth into the newness of gospel life (compare Romans 6:4), since the older customs are plainly overturned, and what was in shadows and types no longer has power to prevail. This was the purpose of his coming into this world. He came to proclaim, to the people of Israel before all others, that what was imposed until the time of reformation (compare Hebrews 9:10), that is, the law in letters, now at last comes to its end, as the mind of believers is remolded, as I said, into what is better and into a spiritual way of life. For all things in Christ are new (compare 2 Corinthians 5:17).

Yet though they ought to have been persuaded by him, the leaders of the synagogue of the Jews above all, who boasted not a little of the glories of the priesthood, opposed him headlong, worked against him impiously, and, though always talking of the law given through the most wise Moses, wanted to make of no effect, as far as it lay with them, the mystery of the Only-Begotten’s economy in the flesh …

title: Uzziah, Ahaz, and the Philistines
english: … strength. At any rate, he besieged, took, and sacked many cities of the Philistines (the “foreigners,” that is, the people of Palestine), and some of those of what is called Coele-Syria. It is written of him thus in the Second Book of Chronicles: “He went out and fought against the foreigners, and overpowered the walls of Gath and the walls of Azotus, and built cities of Azotus and among the foreigners. And the Lord strengthened him against the foreigners and against the Arabs who dwelt on the Rock, and against the Minaeans. And the Minaeans gave gifts to Uzziah, and his name spread as far as the entrance of Egypt, for he grew exceedingly strong” (2 Chronicles 26:6–8).

When he died, Jotham, his son, succeeded to his kingdom. Then after him came Ahaz, a wicked and apostate man who had sunk into the swamps of deceit. For he worshiped wood and stones and all the host of heaven, and he made his son pass through fire, for he sacrificed him to the demons.

It is written of him thus in the Second Book of Kings: “He did not do what was right in the eyes of the Lord his God faithfully, as David his father had done. He walked in the way of the kings of Israel, and even made his son pass through fire, according to the abominations of the nations whom the Lord drove out before the sons of Israel. He burned incense on the high places, and on the hills, and under every leafy tree. Then Rezin king of Syria and Pekah son of Remaliah, king of Israel, came up against Jerusalem to war, and they besieged Ahaz, but could not prevail” (2 Kings 16:2–5). And after other things: “Ahaz sent messengers to Tiglath-pileser king of the Assyrians, saying, ‘I am your servant and your son. Come up and save me from the hand of the king of Syria and from the hand of the king of Israel, who are rising up against me.’ And Ahaz took the silver and gold found in the treasuries of the house of the Lord and of the king’s house, and sent gifts to the king. And the king of the Assyrians listened to him, and came to Damascus, and took it, and carried its people into exile, and put Rezin to death” (2 Kings 16:7–9).

So first Uzziah, also called Azariah, ravaged the foreigners, laid waste all their land, and collected tribute and taxes from them. Second, after him, Ahaz hired the Assyrian and let him loose on them. He uprooted the whole country of the Palestinians (for these, he says, are the foreigners) and carried off to his own land as captives those who were left from the war. When Ahaz died, the cities of the foreigners leapt for joy at it, as though the one who struck them had been taken out of the way, and as if unbearable …

title: A Man Sent to Save Egypt
english: … since they had not come to know the Master of all, would they have cried out to him at all? But just as the blood of Abel is said to have cried out to God (Genesis 4:10), not, surely, as though it had a voice of its own, but because God abhorred the very outrage of the deed, in the same way, I think, one might understand it also of those who used to worship the unclean demons. For even if they do not know the God of all, yet because they have been wronged by Satan, through the deed itself, in a manner, they have cried aloud, surely asking for help for themselves.

In this sense we say that the Egyptians too cried out to God because of those who oppressed them, that is, those who had brought them under their own hand and crushed them as with a most bitter slavery: plainly, the unclean demons. “But the Lord will send them a man who will save them” (Isaiah 19:20). And who is the man, if not, plainly, Christ, that is, the only-begotten Word of God who appeared in human form? He saved not only the Egyptians but the whole earth.

And he saved by judging. What does “by judging” mean? It means that he brought a just judgment in their case. For Satan, who had wronged them, and with him the unclean demons, he subjected to holy verdicts, cast them into Tartarus with chains of gloom, and handed them over to be kept for punishment at the judgment of the great day (compare 2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6). But those who had endured so unbearable a wrong he saved and rescued, and made them his own worshipers, flashing on them the light of truth and clothing them with the glories of freedom.

So the Savior himself says somewhere: “Now is the judgment of this world. Now the ruler of this world will be cast out. And I, if I am lifted up, will draw all to myself” (John 12:31–32). You see that he has given judgment for the world, cast out Satan, who long ago tyrannized over it, and drawn all to himself. For the Egyptians too have come to know him. And indeed, having come to know him, they offer sacrifices, they make vows, and they carry out what they promised (compare Isaiah 19:21). This is what is sung through the voice of David: “Make vows and pay them to the Lord our God” (Psalm 76:11).

See, then, the newness of things. Those who formerly used to sacrifice to demons, who brought their worship to Satan and dedicated thank offerings to him, and who eagerly fulfilled vows, that is, promises, will be enlightened in mind through Christ and made bright by the doctrines of truth. They will run from their ancient error, and having once come to know the Maker and Lord of all, they bring him worship in spirit, fulfilling most pure vows and offering sacrifices no longer through blood and the slaughter of irrational animals …
